correctness.rationale: The odd-candidate bound for pi includes the prime 2 separately. The modulo 6 and 30 bounds count at most two or eight residues per full or final partial block and add the exceptional primes. In the prime and prime-square branches the odd-candidate bound is strictly less than the totient for p>=5, and direct evaluations at p=2,3 leave 3 and 9. For distinct p<q with p>=5, twice the totient minus the divisor sum is (p-3)(q-3)-8, strictly positive except at (5,7), which fails directly. For p=3 the modulo 6 inequality forces q<=11, and for p=2 the modulo 30 inequality forces q<=64. My independent trial-division table agrees with all 21 rows of small_cases.csv; (2,17) is the only equality, with pi(54)=16. The symbolic cutoff and checked finite part exhaust the stated domain; the claimed large sweep is not needed.
residual_risks: No inference about Omega(n)>=3 and no fresh replay of the large frozen sweep.

value.rationale: This is an unbounded theorem for the first two natural multiplicative layers of an established arithmetic equation, not a report of a new finite sweep or an arbitrary numerical cutoff. It proves there are no additional solutions of those types and reduces their determination to a reproducible small exact table.
residual_risks: The proof is elementary and makes no claim about the much larger remaining part of the sequence or about broader prime-counting phenomena.
